title: Parity is associated with cognitive function and brain age in both females and males
abstract: Previous studies of the association between parity and long-term cognitive changes have primarily focused on women and have shown conflicting results. We investigated this association by analyzing data collected on 303,196 subjects from the UK Biobank. We found that in both females and males, having offspring was associated with a faster response time and fewer mistakes made in the visual memory task. Subjects with two or three children had the largest differences relative to those who were childless, with greater effects observed in men. We further analyzed the association between parity and relative brain age (n = 13,584), a brain image-based biomarker indicating how old one's brain structure appears relative to peers. We found that in both sexes, subjects with two or three offspring had significantly reduced brain age compared to those without offspring, corroborating our cognitive function results. Our findings suggest that lifestyle factors accompanying having offspring, rather than the physical process of pregnancy experienced only by females, contribute to these associations and underscore the importance of studying such factors, particularly in the context of sex.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2020 Scientific Reports article has attracted substantial scholarly attention, with 75 OpenAlex citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of works. Its influence is also visible in downstream reuse: the paper has been cited or otherwise reused in 76 documented works, spanning articles, preprints, reviews, book chapters, and an editorial, while scite records indicate a largely supportive citation profile with some explicit disagreement.

Full narrative

Ning and colleagues examined whether parity is associated with cognitive function and brain age in both females and males, using data from the UK Biobank. The study is notable for extending the question beyond women alone and for reporting that having offspring was associated with faster response time and fewer mistakes in a visual memory task in both sexes, with the largest differences observed among those with two or three children. That framing appears to have resonated: the article has accumulated 75 citations and is positioned in the top 10% of works in its field and publication year.

The citation record suggests sustained engagement across the years after publication, with uptake appearing in 2021 through 2026 and peaking in multiple years rather than fading after an initial burst. The citing literature is broad but still centered on related areas of aging, cognition, reproductive history, brain function, and women’s health, indicating that the article has been used as part of ongoing conversations about how reproductive experience may relate to later-life cognitive outcomes and brain aging.

The downstream reuse pattern reinforces that role. Most reusers are journal articles, but the paper is also taken up in preprints, reviews, book chapters, and an editorial, which points to continued methodological and conceptual relevance rather than a single isolated citation trail. Recent citing works show the topic remaining active in adjacent research on brain age, parity, reproductive history, and neurocognitive outcomes, including studies focused on women’s aging, maternal health, and broader life-history questions.

There is also evidence of public-facing discussion, though it is limited in scope: one web mention was captured from a Substack post that used the paper as a springboard for discussing whether childbearing changes the brain or whether pre-existing differences shape family size. The article is open access and supported by Medical Research Council funding, which likely helped make the work broadly available and reusable. Overall, the record shows a well-cited, widely reused paper that has become part of a growing interdisciplinary literature on reproduction, cognition, and brain aging.
